summary: "Surveyor 3: Three Bounces and a Trench" is a pilot episode of an animated series that turns dry space data into stories kids remember. Narrated in the first person by the Surveyor 3 lander (1967), it follows a machine sent to answer one question: can the Moon's ground hold a spacecraft? Three bounces, a trench, a two-week deadline, and an unexpected reunion with Apollo 12 turn mission facts into an adventure for ages 8-12.
details:
THE PROBLEM

NASA has left hardware on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space since the 1960s. Kids usually meet space history through astronauts, while the machines that went first stay invisible. Facts on their own are easy to forget.

OUR APPROACH

We tell the science through story. Knowledge tied to emotion is remembered better, so every episode uses real dramatic tools: a narrator with a voice, a question, a deadline, a turn and a payoff. The machine speaks about itself, and the facts arrive as events in its life.

PILOT: SURVEYOR 3

Before Apollo, scientists feared the Moon's surface might be deep, soft dust that would swallow a lander. Surveyor 3 landed on April 20, 1967, after bouncing twice before settling on the third touchdown. Its scoop dug a trench whose walls held their shape, like damp sand: the ground could hold a crew. About two weeks later night fell and the lander went silent. Thirty-one months after its landing, Apollo 12 touched down less than two football fields away. Astronauts removed its camera, scoop and pieces of tubing to study how the Moon affects metal. The camera is now part of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum collection. The pilot also explains why dust from Apollo 12's landing turned the white lander brown.

WHAT KIDS TAKE AWAY

The Moon's ground is strong enough to land on. A lunar day lasts roughly two weeks, then comes roughly two weeks of night. Pieces of space hardware can come back and be seen in a museum. Behind every dry fact there is an engineering decision and a person who made it.

THE SERIES

The pilot is a format that scales. Next episodes could cover: Ranger 6 (1964), a failed mission whose lessons led to later triumphs; Opportunity on Mars, working long past its planned lifetime and ending its mission in a dust storm; Voyager 1, still travelling away from Earth; and the Apollo laser reflectors, hardware left on the Moon that scientists still use. Each ends with the same question: "More machines are still out there. Which ones?"

WHO IT IS FOR

School-age space enthusiasts (about 10-12), teachers, and science museums that want a short entry point before a visit.

USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)

Humans: the idea, dramaturgy, script, video editing, and sound design.

AI tools:

  • Claude and Gemini: editing and translation of text, and checking our script for factual and wording errors.
  • ElevenLabs: synthetic voiceover for the narrator.
  • Claude Code: generating animation fragments, which were assembled into the final video in an editor.

Fact-checking: every fact in the script was checked against official sources by a team member. AI suggestions were treated as drafts. Example: our early line said nobody knew whether the ground would hold, but Luna 9 and Surveyor 1 had already landed safely, so we changed it to say nobody knew how strong the ground was.
